inline.s: He displayed skill in reckoning, letters, and archery. He broadly mastered the arts and techniques, and studied through the manifold scriptures.
[Commentary]

This is the mark of the fifth youth. Within it there are two parts. First, his person was complete in every skill, meaning he displayed such matters as reckoning, letters, and the like. The Buddha had long known these, but conforming to the transformation he began to learn them, and so it is called "displayed." Second, from "broadly mastered" (bo zong) onward is the breadth of his knowledge and understanding. "Broadly mastered the arts and techniques": this is breadth in knowledge of affairs; "broad" means extensive, "master" means thorough practice. The secret arts of the immortals were all thoroughly learned by him, hence "broadly mastered the arts and techniques." "Studied through the manifold scriptures": this is breadth in knowledge of the teachings; "study through" means penetrating to the end, "studied" means fully mastered. The secular and heterodox classics are called the "manifold scriptures." Of all these he had complete knowledge, hence "studied through the manifold scriptures." This concludes the fifth.
He roamed in the rear garden, discoursing on martial skill and testing his arts. He dwelt within the palace, amid the sensations of form and flavor.
[Commentary]

This is the mark of the sixth, the taking of a wife. Within it, first it says he roamed in the rear garden, discoursing on martial skill and testing his arts: these are matters antecedent to the taking of a wife, as related in the account of his origin. Reining the horse and exerting his sinews is called "discoursing on martial skill"; jointly shooting at the metal drum is spoken of as "testing his arts." "He dwelt within the palace, amid the sensations of form and flavor": these are matters subsequent to the taking of a wife. The Buddha was in truth free of attachment, but conforming to the transformation he displayed this dwelling, hence it is called "he dwelt." A question is asked: why did he display this mark, first receiving and then relinquishing it? To reveal that desire is to be loathed. This concludes the sixth.

Seeing old age, sickness, and death, he awakened to the impermanence of the world. He abandoned the kingdom, its wealth, and his station, and entered the mountains to study the Way. He mounted the white horse with jeweled crown and garland of pearls, then sent them back. He cast aside his precious and fine raiment and donned the robe of Dharma. He shaved off beard and hair, and sat upright beneath the Bodhi tree. Painfully he toiled for six years, doing what was fitting to be done.
[Commentary]

This is the mark of the seventh, the going forth from home. Within it are six phrases, which combine into three pairs. The six phrases are: seeing old age, sickness, and death; awakening to the impermanence of the world; and abandoning the kingdom, its wealth, and his station. This is the first phrase, making clear what he relinquished. As related in the account of his origin, going out of the city to roam and observe, at the eastern gate he saw the aged, at the southern gate the sick, at the western gate the dead. Taking these as likened to himself, he awakened to the impermanence of his body, and so there arose loathing and renunciation; abandoning the kingdom, its wealth, and his station, he entered the mountains to study the Way. This is the second phrase, revealing what he undertook. At the northern gate he saw a wandering monk (shramana); through seeing the shramana he therefore sought to study the Way. The text omits this for brevity. These form one pair. "He mounted the white horse with jeweled crown and garland of pearls, then sent them back; he cast aside his precious and fine raiment": this is the third phrase, again making clear what he relinquished. "And donned the robe of Dharma": this is the fourth phrase, revealing what he received. These form the second pair. "He shaved off beard and hair": this is the fifth phrase, again making clear what he relinquished. "He sat upright beneath the Bodhi tree": this is the sixth phrase, making clear what he did, and also making clear what he cultivated. "Painfully he toiled for six years": first he shared in the heterodox practices; "doing what was fitting to be done." Turning away from heterodox learning, the right Way is what is fitting for him to cultivate and study, and he followed it in practice. These form the third pair. This concludes the seventh mark.

From here on is the eighth mark, the accomplishment of the Buddha-Way. Within it, following the events, there are five in sequence: first, bathing and washing away the stains of the body; second, from "the spirit birds" below, going to the place of the Way; third, from "auspicious" below, receiving the grass and sitting peacefully; fourth, from "he roused great" below, the spiritual power that subdues Mara; fifth, from "he attained the subtle" below, the manifest accomplishment of the Buddha-Way.

He appeared in the five defilements' world, conforming to the multitude of beings, and displayed the dust and grime [of the body]. He bathed in the golden stream; the devas pressed down the branches of the tree, and he gained their support to climb out of the pool.
[Commentary]

Within the first part there are three phrases. First, dwelling in the defiled world, he displayed the presence of dust and grime. As it speaks of the five defilements: the first is the defilement of life-span, in that the retribution of life is short and hasty; the second is the defilement of beings, in that people have no good conduct; the third is the defilement of afflictions, in that the various bonds grow ever stronger; the fourth is the defilement of views, in that false views burn fiercely; the fifth is the defilement of the age, in that famine, pestilence, and the weapons of war arise together. The impure world possesses these, and so it is called the five defilements' world. The Buddha appeared dwelling within it, conforming to the multitude of beings, and displayed the presence of dust and grime. Second, "he bathed in the golden stream": in the river of golden sand he bathed and washed away the stains and grime of the body; this is called "bathed in the golden stream." Third, "the devas pressed down the branches of the tree," and he climbed them to come out of the pool.
The spirit birds flew in attendance as he went to the place of the Way.
[Commentary]

Within the second passage, "the spirit birds flying in attendance, he went to the place of the Way" is as the scripture tells: five hundred bluebirds followed behind the Buddha. This is called "the birds flying in attendance." These are all spirit birds, so they are termed "spirit birds." The place where the Buddha attained the Way is called "the place of the Way" (bodhimaṇḍa), just as the place where wheat is dressed is called the wheat field, and the place where grain is dressed is spoken of as the grain field. And so with all things.
Auspiciousness came as a portent, manifesting the merit and blessing. He compassionately received the offered grass and spread it beneath the Bodhi tree, and sat cross-legged.
[Commentary]

Within the third passage, first he was moved by an auspicious sign which came as a portent. This auspicious one was the grass-cutter; in the scripture he is also named Jiana, for auspiciousness and peace are of the same meaning. As the Buddha was about to accomplish the Way, he was moved by the sight of this man as a portent, knowing that he was surely to accomplish the fruit of auspiciousness, and therefore it is named "auspicious portent." By this very man he manifested the merit and blessing of the fruit he was to accomplish, and so it is named "manifesting merit and blessing." Next, he received the grass: the Buddha's heart was compassionate, and his person received the grass, and so it is named "compassionately received the offered grass." Afterward he spread it and sat. Depending on the tree he attained Buddhahood, and so it is called "the Bodhi tree." Spreading it beneath this tree he sat cross-legged. Now, this is in accordance with the differing seeing and hearing of beings. If one discusses bodhisattvas, they see the Tathagata rising from the vajra-ground with the vajra-seat, going up to the place of the Way, and dwelling there to accomplish Buddhahood, as the Nirvana Sutra states. The common person and the two vehicles only see the Tathagata receive the grass of the auspicious one and spread it as a seat, as said in this text.
He roused forth the great radiance, making Mara aware of it. Mara led his retinue and came to press and test him. He subdued them by wisdom and power, causing them all to be vanquished.
[Commentary]

Within the fourth passage, first "he roused forth the great radiance, making Mara aware of it": "roused forth" (fen) is like releasing. Next, Mara came to press and test him; below, the Buddha subdued him. As to "by wisdom and power": this is the virtue of subduing Mara. Wisdom is the right wisdom, knowing that what is false is not to be followed; power is transcendent power, the spiritual power that subdues Mara. It may also be the power of compassion, the compassionate mind that subdues Mara, causing them all to be vanquished. This is the capacity to subdue Mara. Mara is a barbarian word; here it is translated "killer," because it harms the good of beings. Generally it is spoken of in four categories; the Nirvana Sutra speaks of eight. As to the four: the first is the Mara of afflictions, namely greed, hatred, and the like, which can harm good dharmas; the second is the Mara of the aggregates, namely the body of the five aggregates, mutually destroying one another; the third is the Mara of death, which can destroy the root of life; the fourth is the Mara of the heavens, for upon the sixth heaven of self-transformation there is another heaven of Mara, which is ever ruining the good of others. Of these four, the first is the cause of birth-and-death; the last, the heaven of Mara, is the condition of birth-and-death; the middle two, the aggregates and death, are the fruit of birth-and-death. These four categories are spoken of commonly by both great and small vehicles. As to the eight: upon the former four are added the four inverted minds of the unconditioned, which toward the Buddha's true virtue regard the eternal as impermanent, the happy as suffering, the self as no-self, and the pure as impure. With these four, in a near sense they destroy right understanding, and in a distant sense they obstruct true virtue, and so they are called Maras. These latter four are not regarded as afflictions in the small vehicle, and so it does not speak of them as Maras; in the great vehicle they are faults, and so it speaks of them as Maras. In general, discussing these eight, all must be subdued. Why is this so? The afflictions, aggregates, death, and the four inverted minds of the unconditioned obstruct one's own practice, and so they must be subdued. The modes of subduing differ. As to the Mara of afflictions, the small vehicle mostly uses contemplative contemplation to subdue it, and the great vehicle mostly uses the wisdom of emptiness to subdue it. As to the Maras of the aggregates and of death, the small vehicle mostly subdues them by the nirvana of no residue, because it achieves extinction, while the great vehicle mostly subdues them by the eternal Dharma-body. As to the four inverted minds of the unconditioned, within the great cause they are subdued by right understanding, and within the great fruit they are subdued by the true virtue of bodhi and nirvana. The single Mara of the heavens obstructs both one's own practice and the transformation of others, and so it must be subdued. The means used differ: within the cause of one's own practice it is subdued by right wisdom, for knowing that what is false is not to be followed, it retreats and disperses of itself; within the essential of one's own practice it is subdued by the ten powers, for the ten powers are firm and are not to be toppled by Mara and falsehood. Since one's own practice is thus, within the transformation of others the means are not fixed. If one is in the cause, subduing Mara oneself for the benefit of beings, one mostly uses transcendent power; when teaching others to subdue Mara, one mostly uses the divine mantra, for they have no spiritual power to subdue it. If one is in the fruit, subduing Mara oneself for the benefit of beings, one mostly uses the compassionate mind, and out of compassion for them they retreat and disperse; when teaching others to subdue Mara, one also uses the divine mantra, for they have no power of compassion to subdue it. What is discussed here is the specific subduing of the heaven of Mara. In violating one's own practice, right wisdom subdues it; in violating the benefit of others, transcendent power subdues it. Hence it is said "by wisdom and power he caused them all to be vanquished."
He attained the subtle Dharma and accomplished the highest right awakening.
[Commentary]

Within the fifth passage, "he attained the subtle Dharma and accomplished the highest right awakening": this is the manifest accomplishment of Buddhahood. The principle is the subtle Dharma; because he attained this Dharma he accomplished right awakening. This concludes the eighth mark.
From here on is the ninth mark, the turning of the Dharma-wheel. First, there is the request, and afterward the teaching.
Brahma and Indra prayed and urged, requesting that he turn the Dharma-wheel.
[Commentary]
This is the first, the request.

From here on, because of the request, he arose and taught. Within it there are two: first, the transformation arising through body and speech; second, from "with the Buddha's roaming tread, the Buddha's roar, he roared" below, and the radiance universally illuminating the countless lands, the body and speech that gather in and benefit.

With the Buddha's roaming tread he trod; with the Buddha's roar he roared. He beat the drum of Dharma, blew the conch of Dharma, wielded the sword of Dharma, raised the banner of Dharma, thundered the thunder of Dharma, flashed the lightning of Dharma, rained the rain of Dharma, and performed the gift of Dharma. Ever with the sound of Dharma he awakened all worlds.
[Commentary]

Within the former, first it says "with the Buddha's roaming tread he trod": this is the transformation arising through the body's action, displaying the Buddha's dignified deportment, roaming and transforming beings. It is called "the Buddha's roaming tread." From "the Buddha's roar he roared" onward is the transformation arising through speech action. Within it are ten phrases. The single phrase "with the Buddha's roar he roared" is the summary; all the sacred teachings are what the Buddha roars, and the bodhisattva uses them as a roar for beings. The eight phrases from "he beat the drum" onward are the particulars, using similes to reveal the Dharma. Of these, the first four are the four dharmas of hearing, reflection, cultivation, and realization. "He beat the drum of Dharma": this teaches the Dharma of the wisdom of hearing, benefiting beings. A drum is solemnly beaten to warn the troops, so teaching by precept warns people. "He blew the conch of Dharma": this teaches the Dharma of the wisdom of reflection, benefiting beings. The conch is blown in due season, so speaking the principle answers the occasion. "He wielded the sword of Dharma": this teaches the Dharma of the wisdom of cultivation, benefiting beings. The sword can split apart, so cultivation can sever the bonds. "He raised the banner of Dharma": this openly proclaims the Dharma of realization; the Dharma of realization is lofty and surpassing, like a banner rising above. The last four are the four unobstructed knowledges, arising to teach and benefiting beings. "He thundered the thunder of Dharma": this is the Dharma-unobstructed wisdom transforming beings. Once the heavenly thunder moves, plants and grasses sprout; once the sound of Dharma is heard, the Way is quickly accomplished. "He flashed the lightning of Dharma": this is the meaning-unobstructed wisdom benefiting beings. Once the lightning flashes, creatures see it; once the meaning is proclaimed, all meanings are seen. "He rained the rain of Dharma": this is the expression-unobstructed wisdom transforming beings. Using expression to proclaim, like clouds sending down rain. "He performed the gift of Dharma": this is the joy-of-teaching unobstructed wisdom benefiting beings. According to what beings delight in, he proclaims and bestows, which is called "performed the gift of Dharma." These eight are the particulars. The single phrase "ever with the sound of Dharma he awakened all worlds" is the summary. Up to this point is the first, the transformation arising through body and speech.

From here on is the second, the gathering in and benefiting through body and speech. Within it there are four: first, the body's action subduing Mara, causing beings to abandon false livelihood; second, from "he rent and tore" below, the speech action destroying false views, causing beings to abandon afflictions. These form one pair. Third, from "entering the kingdom and begging" below, the body's action receiving offerings, producing the merit and good of beings; fourth, from "wishing to proclaim the Dharma" below, the speech action teaching the Dharma, causing beings to cultivate the path of transcendence. These form one pair.

The radiance universally illuminated the countless Buddha-lands, and all worlds trembled in six ways. He gathered in all the realm of Mara, moved the palace of Mara, and all the troops of Mara, seized with terror, had none who did not submit.
[Commentary]

Within the first part there are four: first, emitting radiance that universally illuminates the countless Buddha-lands; second, by spiritual power causing all worlds to tremble in six ways; third, because of the previous radiance, gathering in all the realm of Mara, causing them all to submit; fourth, because of the previous trembling, moving the palace of Mara and causing it fear and dread.

He rent and tore the net of falsehood, destroyed all the [false] views, scattered all the dust and toil, ruined all the moat of desire, guarded the city of Dharma, opened wide the gate of Dharma, washed away the stains and defilement, made manifest the pure and bright, let the Dharma of Buddhahood shine, and broadly flowed forth the right transformation.
[Commentary]

Within the second, the speech action, the text also has four. First, it is able to destroy the false: "he rent and tore the net of falsehood" is the breaking of false dharmas; "destroyed all the [false] views" teaches the severing of the false mind. These two remove the views. "He scattered all the dust and toil" is the destruction of the objects of desire; the objects of the five desires can be defiling dust that toils and disorders beings, and so they are called "dust and toil." He speaks emptiness to destroy and reject them, and this is termed "scattered." "He ruined all the moat of desire" teaches the relinquishing of the mind of desire. The mind of love and desire is deep and hard to cross, and so it is spoken of as a "moat"; teaching its severance is called "ruin." These two remove love. These four pairs together form the first, making clear he is able to destroy the false. Second, from "he guarded" onward makes clear he is able to open up the right. "He guarded the city of Dharma" wards off slander of it by people; the Dharma can guard and ward off, and so it is spoken of as a "city." Praising the good and stilling slander is called "guard" and "protect." "He opened wide the gate of Dharma": he proclaims the right teaching, and the total Dharma has the meaning of a path of entry and approach, and so it is called a "gate." Spreading and drawing beings in is called "open" and "wide." Third, from "he washed" below gathers up the previous first meaning of destroying the false: the afflictions of views and love are called "stains and defilement," and teaching their removal is called "washed." Fourth, from "he made manifest" below reveals the previous second meaning of opening up the right: "made manifest the pure and bright, let the Dharma of Buddhahood shine" reveals the previous phrase of "guarding the city of Dharma." Removing the false and revealing the right, so it is called "made manifest." The Dharma made manifest, transcending false slander, is called "pure and bright." Displaying the right Dharma, going forth from the false and depraved, is called "shine." Merging and ordering it to purity is called "let the Dharma of Buddhahood shine." "He broadly flowed forth the right transformation" reveals the previous phrase of "opening wide the gate of Dharma," broadly flowing to transform beings, and so it is called "opened wide." This concludes the first pair.
Entering the kingdom he begged for food, guarding the abundant meals. He stored up merit and revealed the field of blessing.
[Commentary]

Within the third, the body. "Entering the kingdom he begged for food": this is beginning the practice of begging. "Begging" (fen wei) is a barbarian word; here it is translated "begging for food." He obtained the abundant meals, for through begging he obtained food. From "he stored up merit" onward is the receiving and using that produces blessing. "Stored up" (chu) means to accumulate; storing and accumulating many meritorious virtues is called "stored up merit." Now he received offerings of things, hence it is named "revealed." It produces the merit and good of the world, and the field that produces things to the body is therefore called "field of blessing."

Wishing to proclaim the Dharma, he manifested a joyful smile. With all the medicines of Dharma he healed and saved the three sufferings. He manifested the meaning of the Way, the immeasurable merits, and bestowed the prediction [of Buddhahood] upon the bodhisattvas, causing them to accomplish the right awakening.
[Commentary]

Within the fourth, the speech. "Wishing to proclaim, he manifested a smile": this is the skillful means of beginning the teaching. Below is the correct teaching. Within it, first it says "with all the medicines of Dharma he healed and saved the three sufferings," causing beings to transcend birth-and-death. The suffering of suffering, the suffering of decay, and the suffering of conditioning: these are the three sufferings. Their meaning is as in the separate chapter; this should be fully discussed. He bestows the teaching and instructs their severance, which is called "medicine and healing." From "he manifested" onward causes beings to enter the Way. Within it, first "he manifested the meaning of the Way" teaches beings to rouse the resolve, manifesting the aspiring mind of the Way which the bodhisattvas have roused, and causing beings to rouse it. "The immeasurable merits" teaches beings to practice. From "bestowing the prediction upon the bodhisattvas" onward finally causes them to attain the fruit. "Bestowing the prediction upon the bodhisattvas" is the means of attaining the fruit; practicing the cause and reaching the fruit is like the mind recording things, and so it is called a "prediction." The Sage's teaching showing it to beings is termed "bestowing." "Causing them to accomplish the right awakening" is the manifest accomplishment of Buddhahood. This concludes the ninth mark.
He displayed the passing into extinction, saving and delivering without limit, eradicating all the outflows, and planting the root of virtue.
[Commentary]

This is the tenth mark, the parinirvana. "He displayed the passing into extinction" is the manifest taking of extinction. Below is the benefit it reveals. "Saving and delivering without limit" reveals the broadness of the benefit. "Eradicating the outflows, etc." reveals the completeness of the benefit. Eradicating all the outflows: because of the manifest extinction, it causes beings to loathe existence and sever the cause of birth-and-death. Planting the root of virtue: because of the manifest extinction, it causes beings to rejoice in stillness and cultivate the cause of nirvana. This concludes the tenth mark.
The above broadly praises the two virtues, the provisional and the real.
Complete in virtue, subtle and hard to measure, he roamed in the various Buddha-lands and universally manifested the teaching of the Way.
[Commentary]

This is the third, the pair that gathers them up. "Complete in virtue, subtle and hard to measure" gathers up the previous real virtue. "He roamed in the various Buddha-lands and universally manifested the teaching of the Way" gathers up the previous provisional virtue. This is the provisional and real virtue.
The Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha's Teaching on the Immeasurable Life, Scroll One, end.

blocks.text: The Commentary on the Sutra of the Buddha's Teaching on the Immeasurable Life, Scroll Two

inline.s: From here on is the second, praising the merit of benefiting self and benefiting others. Practice that can benefit oneself is called "benefiting self"; practice that can also moisten others is called "benefiting others." The practice of the bodhisattva in essentials does not go beyond these, and so they are praised. Within it, first is a brief praise; from "the bodhisattvas' scriptures" onward is the broad praise.

Their cultivation was pure and without defilement, like a magician displaying many different forms, becoming male or female, with nothing he does not transform. Having clearly learned the original [arts], he does as he wills. These bodhisattvas are likewise: they study all dharmas, penetrating and thoroughly refining them; what they dwell in is peaceful and true, and there is nothing they do not influence. In countless Buddha-lands they are all universally present. Never were they proud or indulgent. Commiserating with beings, they are fully possessed of such dharmas.
[Commentary]

Within the brief [praise], first are the particulars, and afterward the summary. Within the particulars there are four: first, the purity of one's own practice; second, from "like a magician" below is the skillfulness of transformative practice, first with a simile and then the matching. Within the simile, first it says "like a magician": this is the simile for the one who rouses transformation. "Displaying many different forms, becoming male or female, etc." is the simile for the marks of the roused transformation. "Having clearly learned the original [arts], etc." is the simile for the virtue of the roused transformation. "Having clearly learned the original [arts]" is the simile for studying the dharmas of transformation; learning is the basis of transformation, hence it is called "original" (ben). In the Buddha's dharmas of transformation, mastering them well is called "clearly learned." "He does as he wills" means that when learning is accomplished, the function arises; the accomplishment lies in the mind, hence it is called "as he wills." Transforming at will is called "does." Below is the matching that reveals the Dharma. "These bodhisattvas are likewise" matches the previous magician. "They study all dharmas, etc." matches the virtue of the roused transformation. "They study all dharmas" matches the previous "clearly learned," meaning they study all the dharmas of transforming others. "Penetrating and thoroughly refining them" matches "clearly learned": penetrating, mastering, knowing the dharmas thoroughly and fully, hence "thoroughly refining." "What they dwell in is peaceful and true" matches "as he wills": in the dharmas in which they dwell they rest the mind in peace and true contemplation. "There is nothing they do not influence" matches "he does": "nothing" (mi) means there is no; "influence" (zhi) means to convey, so in every place there is nothing they do not convey in transformation. Also, "influence" is their moving the influence [of their teaching], causing all beings to have nothing they do not influence. "In countless Buddha-lands they are all universally present" matches the previous marks of transformation, matching "displaying many forms, becoming male or female, etc." This is the second, the skillfulness of transformative practice. Third, from "never were they proud" below reveals the previous first, the purity of one's own practice: because of what they attained, never were they high and proud in self-indulgence, so their practice is pure. Fourth, from "commiserating" below reveals the previous second, the skillfulness of transformative practice. "Commiserating" is compassion. Having a compassionate heart, commiserating with beings, they are therefore able to display various transformations for beings. The above is the particular praise. "Such dharmas, fully possessed" is the summary that gathers them up. The above is the brief praise.

Below is the broad praise. Within it there are four: first, relying on the bodhisattva dharmas to cultivate the practice belonging to one's own share; second, from "the immeasurable Buddhas altogether protect" below, relying on the Buddha dharmas to cultivate the surpassing advance; third, from "making offerings to the Buddhas" below, relying on the previous own-share to cultivate broadly and realize virtue; fourth, from "receiving and maintaining the Tathagata's deeply profound Dharma-treasury" below, relying on the previous surpassing advance to distinguish and realize virtue.
The bodhisattvas' scriptures: they deeply penetrated the essential and subtle. Their fame reached everywhere, and they guided and governed the ten directions.
[Commentary]

Within the first passage, first is the cultivation of benefiting self, and afterward the arising of benefiting others. "The bodhisattvas' scriptures they deeply penetrated the essential and subtle" is the benefiting of self. In the bodhisattva dharmas they thoroughly penetrated and were unobstructed, attaining their essential aim and knowing their subtle purport, and so it is called "deeply penetrated the essential and subtle." "Their fame reached everywhere and they guided and governed the ten directions" is the benefiting of others.

The immeasurable Buddhas altogether protected and kept them in mind. What the Buddha dwells in, they had all already attained. What the great Sages established, they had all established. The Tathagata's teaching and transformation each they could proclaim; for the various bodhisattvas they became great teachers. With the profoundly deep meditation and wisdom they opened and guided beings; they penetrated the nature of all dharmas, reached the marks of beings, and were clear about the various lands.
[Commentary]

Within the second passage, it is also first the benefiting of self; from "the Tathagata's teaching and transformation each they could proclaim" below is the benefiting of others. Within the benefiting of self, "the immeasurable Buddhas protected them": the higher virtue draws in the lower; entering the Buddha's realm, they are therefore protected and kept in mind by all the Buddhas together. Protecting keeps them from evil; keeping in mind causes them to increase in good. From "what the Buddha dwells in, etc." below is the lower practice following the higher. Within it, first "what the Buddha dwells in, they had all already attained": this is the realization of practice identical with the Buddha. What the Buddha dwells in as Dharma, the bodhisattvas dwell in alike; one may also say the various Buddhas dwell in the Thus-practice, and the bodhisattvas dwell in alike. "What the great Sages established, they had all established": this is the teaching-practice identical with the Buddha. "The great Sages" are the Buddhas; the perfections of the Dharma-realm are what the Buddhas established, and the bodhisattvas established them alike. Below, within the benefiting of others, first is the mark of benefiting others; from "they penetrated the various dharmas" below is the virtue of benefiting others. Within the mark of benefiting others, "the Tathagata's teaching and transformation each they could proclaim" and "became teachers for the bodhisattvas" is the teaching the Dharma benefiting people. "The Tathagata's teaching and transformation each they could proclaim" means their teaching of the Dharma was like the Buddha; "for the various bodhisattvas they became great teachers" means their benefitting people was like the Buddha. Now they practice the Buddha's transformation, and so they became great teachers for the bodhisattvas. Again, "with the profoundly deep meditation and wisdom they opened and guided beings": this is the realization of Dharma benefiting beings, for with the profound meditation and wisdom their transformative practice is like the Buddha. Meditation is stopping and wisdom is contemplation; although the realizations of practice are many, in essentials they do not go beyond these. "Opening and guiding beings" means benefitting people is like the Buddha. Below, within the virtue of benefiting others, it makes clear they possess the three kinds of sovereign-practice, and so they can transform beings. "They penetrated the nature of all dharmas" is the sovereign-practice of the knowledge of right awakening; it means they can penetrate the Dharma-nature of the two truths. "They reached the marks of beings" is the sovereign-practice of the world of beings. "Beings" (zhongsheng) — because of manifold deaths they are called "beings"; many dharmas complete their birth, and so they too are called "beings." Whether form or body, all sorts of marks, they know them all. "They were clear about the various lands" is the sovereign-practice of the world of vessels. The first phrase says "penetrated," the second "reached," the third "clear" — these are words [of the same sense] for left and right [variation]. These three are extensively as stated in other scriptures.

From here on is the third, relying on the previous own-share to cultivate broadly and realize virtue. Within it there are four: first, the skillful means of gathering and cultivating; second, from "also there is nothing done" below, realizing virtue through cultivation; third, from "dwelling in deep concentration" below, again making clear the arising of cultivation; fourth, from "surpassing all the things in the world" below, again making clear the realized fruit.

Within the first there are again four: first, cultivating the benefit of self; second, from "rent and tear" below, making clear the benefit of others; third, from "surpassing" below, again making clear the benefit of self; fourth, from "well establishing" below, again making clear the benefit of others. The first passage, benefiting self, makes clear the cultivation of the teaching-practice. The second, benefiting others, teaches beings to leave their faults. The third, benefiting self, makes clear the cultivation of the realization-practice. The fourth, benefiting others, teaches beings to cultivate good. So there are four distinctions.
Making offerings to the Buddhas, he manifested his body like a flash of lightning. He skillfully learned the net of fearlessness, and understood clearly the dharmas of illusion.
[Commentary]

Within the first, benefiting self: "Making offerings to the Buddhas, he manifested his body like a flash of lightning" makes clear the cultivation of the merit-practice. Making offerings to the Buddhas is a broad production of merit. Manifesting the body like lightning is swiftness in rising to practice; in a single thought the transformed body arrives everywhere, making offerings to the Buddhas. From "he skillfully learned" below makes clear the cultivation of the wisdom-practice. "He skillfully learned fearlessness" is the cultivation of the skillful means of wisdom; "understood clearly the dharmas of illusion" is the accomplishment of the wisdom-practice. Again, learning fearlessness, toward people he is undaunted; understanding clearly the dharmas of illusion, toward dharmas he can discern false from right and take the right, which is called "skillfully learned." Reaching the right and passing beyond the false, he is therefore fearless. With the fearless wisdom he gathers in all the dharmas, and so it is called a "net." One may also say that he learns this to use it to gather in people, and so it is said to be a "net." Seeing clearly that all dharmas are free of the nature of being and nonbeing, like illusion and neither existent nor nonexistent, is called "understood clearly the dharmas of illusion." If a dharma were fixedly existent, it could not be called illusorily existent; if a dharma were fixedly nonexistent, it could not be called illusorily nonexistent. The nonexistent taken as existent is what is called illusorily existent; the existent taken as nonexistent is what is called illusorily nonexistent. The nonexistent taken as existent, then the existent is not existent; the existent taken as nonexistent, then the nonexistent is not nonexistent. The illusory dharma is thus, and so it is taken as a simile; transformation is likewise. The scripture speaks of ten similes, all raising this one. The above is the self-benefit; this concludes the first passage.
He rent and tore the net of Mara, and released all the bonds and ties.
[Commentary]

Next, about benefiting others. "He rent and tore the net of Mara" causes beings to leave false livelihood. "He released all the bonds and ties" causes beings to leave afflictions. "Bonds" (chan) are the ten bonds: lack of shame, lack of remorse, sleepiness, regret, miserliness, jealousy, restlessness, hatred, anger, and concealment — these are its ten. Because they bind beings and bind the mind, they are called "bonds." "Ties" (fu) are the four ties: the tie of desire, the tie of existence, the tie of ignorance, and the tie of views — these are its four. The various bonds of the desire-realm, aside from ignorance and views, are called the tie of desire. In the upper two realms, all the afflictions aside from ignorance and views are called the tie of existence. The ignorance of the three realms is called the tie of ignorance. The views of the three realms are called the tie of views. Because they bind beings and bind the mind, they are called "ties." One may also say that all the various bonds of affliction are in general called bonds and ties. The bodhisattva teaches beings to sever and leave them, which is called "released." This concludes the two passages.
He transcended the ground of the voice-hearers and the pratyekabuddhas, and attained the samadhi of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
[Commentary]

From here on is the third, again making clear the benefit of self. "He transcended the ground of the voice-hearers and pratyekabuddhas" is the surpassing excellence of what was cultivated. Here it makes clear the name and meaning of "voice-hearer." Generally explained, there are three. First, the teachings spoken by the Tathagata are called "voice"; hearing the voice and awakening to the understanding, so called "voice-hearer." Second, what is called "self, beings, etc." has only a name and no reality, and so it is spoken of as "voice"; as the Shastra on the Stages says: contemplating this understanding, it is by meaning called "hearing." Third, what the Buddha speaks, the great-vehicle Dharma-sound, is called "voice"; with the Buddha-Way's sound he causes all beings to hear, so called "voice-hearer," as explained in the Lotus Sutra. The former two are small vehicle; the last is great vehicle. Now we discuss the small. Its name and meaning being thus, what are its essence and marks? There are two: one is "voice-hearer among voice-hearers," two is "voice-hearer among pratyekabuddhas"; the meaning is as explained above. As to "pratyekabuddha" (solitary awake), its name and meaning are three: first, the twelve-conditioned dharmas are called "conditions" (yuan); contemplating these he awakens, hence "condition-awakened" (pratyekabuddha), as the Sutra of the Twelve Nidanas says. Second, the events of the present world and their interrelated conditions are called "conditions"; by relying on these he awakens, hence "condition-awakened," as the Sutra of the Pratyekabuddha's Attainment of the Way says. Third, the Dharmarealm of the Tathagata-treasury's dependent-arising is called "conditions"; within it awakening from delusion, hence "condition-awakened." Of the three, the former two are small vehicle; the last is great vehicle. Now we discuss the small. Its name and meaning being thus, what are its aspects? There are two: one is "pratyekabuddha among pratyekabuddhas," two is "pratyekabuddha among voice-hearers." The pratyekabuddha among pratyekabuddhas is one who originally sought the Way of pratyekabuddhas, ever delighting in contemplating the twelve-conditioned dharmas, accomplished in the nature of pratyekabuddha; in his last body, not encountering a Buddha's world, he relies on the conditions of present matters and attains the awakening of the Way, and so he is called "pratyekabuddha among pratyekabuddhas." The pratyekabuddha among voice-hearers is one who originally sought the Way of voice-hearers and accomplished the nature of a voice-hearer; encountering a Buddha who taught him the four true truths, he attained the first fruit, but owing to dull faculties he did not attain to the ending of the outflows; among gods and men he received seven rebirths, and in his last body, not encountering a Buddha's world, he relied on the conditions of present matters and attained the awakening of the Way. Because he was originally a voice-hearer and in his last body, relying on present conditions, attained awakening, he is spoken of as a "pratyekabuddha among voice-hearers." All of these the bodhisattva passes beyond entirely, hence "he transcended." "He attained the samadhi of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness" is the profundity of what was attained, making clear what was entered. Beings and dharmas are wholly without self-nature, hence called "emptiness." Even the conditions also do not exist as marks, called "signlessness." This rejects what is taken; apart from the mind of false thought that takes, hence called "wishlessness." "Samadhi" (sanmei) is a barbarian word, here translated "right concentration." In these three emptinesses, rightly dwelling without disorder, hence "samadhi." From this the name is derived; the meaning has many gates, extensively as in the separate chapter. This should be fully discussed. This concludes the three passages.
He skillfully established skillful means and displayed the three vehicles. Amid these lower and intermediate [vehicles] he manifested the passing into extinction.
[Commentary]

This is the fourth, again making clear the benefit of others. "He skillfully established skillful means" (upaya) is the wisdom of transforming others. The meaning of "skillful means" is generally discussed in four. First, the skillful means of advance and approach, as the seven skillful means before the path of seeing, advancing toward the fruit, hence called "skillful means." Second, the skillful means of practice and creation, as in the ten perfections the perfection of skillful means, skillfully cultivating the various practices, hence "skillful means." Third, the skillful means of provisional dexterity, as in the two knowledges the knowledge of skillful means, provisionally and dexterously gathering in beings, hence "skillful means." Fourth, the skillful means of integration and accomplishment: all dharmas are of one essence, and skillfully integrated and accomplished, hence "skillful means." Thus the Shastra on the Stages says: this Dharma being skillfully accomplished is called "skillful means." And other scriptures speak of the gate of the six marks as "skillful means," and this is also its integrated-accomplishment. What is discussed here is the skillful means of provisional dexterity. Within the provisional dexterity, the skillful means have three: first, the skillful means of body-action, provisionally displaying different forms, as in the case of Avalokitesvara: what is his skillful power? "To those who are to be saved by a Buddha-body he manifests a Buddha-body and teaches them the Dharma," and so with all things. Second, the skillful means of speech-action: conforming to beings, he gives various different teachings, called "skillful means," as when there is no [real] two vehicles and yet he provisionally speaks of them, and so with all things. Third, the skillful means of mind-action: called the knowledge of skillful means, conforming to beings, he gives various different understandings. What is discussed here is the mind-action skillful means within the provisional. Skillfully establishing the three actions and dexterously delivering beings, hence "skillful means." From "he displayed the three" below is the practice of transforming others. "He displayed the three vehicles": this teaches the cause of the three vehicles; dividing the great into small, it is called "displaying the three vehicles." "Amid these lower and intermediate he manifested the passing into extinction": this teaches the fruit of the small vehicle. The pratyekabuddha is called "intermediate"; the voice-hearer is called "lower." In these two he speaks of there being nirvana, called "manifested the passing into extinction." These are all the speech-action skillful means.
The above four passages combine into the first, the cultivation of what is gathered and practiced.

From here on is the second, realizing virtue through cultivation. Within it, first is the merit of benefiting self; from "he proclaimed" below is the virtue of benefiting others. Within the first there are four: first, the equality of what is realized; second, from "complete" below, the many things realized; third, from "broadly still" below, the profundity and breadth of what is realized; fourth, from "he obtained the Buddha's" below, the surpassing excellence of what is realized.
Also there is nothing done, also there is nothing possessed. Neither arising nor ceasing, he attained the Dharma of equality.
[Commentary]

Within "the equality of what is realized," "also there is nothing done": there is no cause that can be made; "also there is nothing possessed": there is no fruit that can be had. As to "nothing arises": there is no pure [dharma] that can arise; as to "nothing ceases": there is no defiled [dharma] that can cease. This raises the principle. "He attained the Dharma of equality": approaching the principle, distinguishing realization; calling the previous "nothing done, nothing possessed, etc." the Dharma of equality, realizing and merging with it is called "attained."
He was complete and accomplished in the immeasurable dharani and the hundreds and thousands of samadhis, and the wisdom of the various faculties.
[Commentary]

Within "the many things realized," "he was complete and accomplished in the immeasurable dharani" means he obtained the dharani, the virtue of practice being many, as other scriptures say. "The hundreds and thousands of samadhis and the wisdom of the various faculties" is the manyness of the remaining virtues. Faith, vigor, mindfulness, etc. are called "the various faculties." If discussed generally, all the good dharmas are wholly called "the various faculties," as the Nirvana Sutra says.
Broadly still and concentrated, he entered deeply into the bodhisattva Dharma-treasury.
[Commentary]

Within making clear the profundity and breadth of what is realized, "broadly still and concentrated" is the breadth of what is realized; in all dharmas no false thought arises, so it is called "broadly still and concentrated." "He entered deeply into the Dharma-treasury" is the profundity of what is realized; into the true Dharma-treasury he can enter deeply.
He obtained the Buddha's Avatamsaka-samadhi.
[Commentary]

Within "the surpassing excellence of what is realized," "he obtained the Buddha Tathagata's Avatamsaka-samadhi," so the virtue is surpassing. The Avatamsaka-samadhi is as the Avatamsaka says: that single samadhi gathers in the whole Dharmarealm, and all the Buddha-dharmas enter within it. The above is the benefit of self.
He proclaimed and expounded all the scriptures.
[Commentary]
Proclaiming and freely communicating all, the benefit of others is to be known.

Dwelling in the gate of deep concentration, he beheld all the immeasurable Buddhas of the present. In an instant, there was nothing he did not reach everywhere. He saved those in the utmost distress; both the untroubled and the troubled places. He distinguished and revealed the true limit, obtained all the Tathagatas' wisdom of eloquence, entered the many sounds and words of [beings], and opened and transformed all.
[Commentary]

This is the third, again making clear the arising of cultivation. "Dwelling in the gate of deep concentration, he beheld all the immeasurable Buddhas of the present, etc." is the cultivation of the benefit of self. "Dwelling in the gate of deep concentration" is the basis from which practice arises. Without a to-and-fro mind, he rises directly by the power of the Dharma-gate of samadhi, and so he must dwell in concentration. Below makes clear the arising of practice. "He beheld all the immeasurable Buddhas of the present" is the breadth of what is gathered in. Because he saw many Buddhas, making offerings produces merit and receiving the Dharma produces wisdom. "In an instant, there was nothing he did not reach everywhere" is the swiftness of the arising of practice. Below makes clear the benefit of others. "He saved those in the utmost distress" and "both the untroubled and the troubled places": this supports people in leaving suffering. The difficulties are separately eight: the three [bad] destinies number three; among humans there are four: the first is blind, deaf, and mute; the second is worldly intelligence, disputatious and clever; the third is in the time before a Buddha and after a Buddha; the fourth is the Uttarakuru realm; among the heavens there is one, namely in the form-realm the heavens of long life apart. Of these eight difficulties, the three [bad] destinies are the most distressed, and the bodhisattva saves them. The suffering of gods and men is slight, and is called "the untroubled places"; the bodhisattva urges and transforms them, and so it is called "the troubled places." "He distinguished and revealed, etc." bestows good dharmas on people. "He distinguished and revealed the true limit" is the realization teaching people; the principle of true reality, the place where it is attained is called the "limit," and bestowing it on people is called "revealed." "He obtained all the Tathagatas' wisdom of eloquence, etc." is the teaching of the Dharma benefiting beings. "He obtained all the Tathagatas' wisdom of eloquence" is the obtaining of the teaching's arising, meaning he obtained the Tathagatas' four unobstructed knowledges and understood all dharmas. "He entered the many sounds and words" is the understanding of the teaching's arising; "entered" means to understand, meaning he understood the various sounds and words of beings and used them to rise up and teach. "He opened and transformed all" is the right revealing of the arising of the teaching.

He surpassed all the things in the world. His mind ever dwelt truly on the Way that delivers the world. Amid all the myriad things, he was free and at ease. He became an uninvited friend to all the manifold classes, bearing the heavy burden for the multitude of beings.
[Commentary]

This is the fourth, again making clear the realized fruit. Within it, first is making clear the accomplishment of the virtue of self; from "amid all things" below is the virtue of benefiting others. Within the self, first "he surpassed all the things in the world" is the surpassing excellence of what was realized. "His mind ever dwelt truly, etc." is the unmoving of what was realized. Again, "he surpassed the world" makes clear the realized virtue of severance, meaning he passed beyond all the dharmas of the world of defilement and transformation. "His mind ever dwelt truly on the Way that delivers the world" makes clear the realized virtue of wisdom. "Truly" (di) means peaceful and true, meaning he ever dwelt peacefully in the true, unconditioned Way that delivers the world. Below, within the benefiting of others, "amid all the myriad things he was free and at ease" is the virtue of benefiting others: because he accomplished the surpassing transcendent power, amid all things he changes and transforms at ease, and so he can benefit beings, which is called "free and at ease." From "he became the friend of the multitudes" below is the arising of the use of benefiting others. "He became an uninvited friend to all the manifold classes" is the skillful means of transformative benefit. "The manifold" (shu) means the common and ordinary; "classes" (lei) means categories. "Uninvited" has two meanings: first, having no root of the Way from of old, yet moved by the bodhisattva, is called "uninvited"; second, having no present delight, not knowing to seek the Sage, is called "uninvited." The bodhisattva becomes a friend to these forcefully. "Bearing the heavy burden for the multitude of beings" is the right making clear of transformative benefit. The voice-hearer abandons beings and does not take the multitude of beings as a heavy burden; the bodhisattva bears and carries them, and so he uses the beings as a heavy burden. The burden has four distinctions, as the Srimala Sutra says. This concludes the third.

From here on is the fourth, relying on the previous surpassing advance to distinguish and realize virtue. Within it, first is distinguishing what is cultivated; from "all the roots of good all crossed over" below makes clear what is realized.
